Engineering

Engineered, simulated, tested.

Every number here comes from our engineering report: simulations, lab tests and hand calculations. Tap View source to see the original figure.

Heel under load

We simulated the stainless-steel heel at 400 N, the force of walking on one foot. It flexes a little, like a spring, and stays within its safety margin.

SolidWorks FEA400 NStainless steel 304
y(x) = −7.124·10⁻⁶x⁵ + 4.95·10⁻⁴x⁴ − 0.01235x³ + 0.1284x² − 0.4508x + 0.6527

A foot traced from an X-ray

We found points along the bones of a healthy foot X-ray in MATLAB and fitted a curve to them. The V8 foot follows that arch.

MATLAB27 cm
Infill60%
Flexural strength39.6 MPa
Stiffness2.49 GPa
Max force129.8 N

Choosing the infill

We printed PLA test bars from 10% to 100% infill and broke them in a bending test. 60% gave the best balance of strength, weight and cost. Tap a bar to compare.

Curves rebuilt from each sample's measured strength, stiffness and breaking strain.

Four-bar knee kinematics

Links of 18.5, 45, 35 and 30 mm. We solved the speeds by hand and checked them in MATLAB: the motor needs 11.3 N·m, so we size it for 16.9 N·m with a 1.5× margin.

MATLAB16.9 N·m
180kN/m

Heel springs sized by hand

To stop a 3,600 N landing within 3 cm, the heel needs about 180 kN/m. Two 90 kN/m springs in parallel give exactly that.

Damping tuned in Simulink

We tuned the foot's damping in Simulink until each step settled smoothly, without bouncing. A damping value of 4,000 gave the most comfortable response.

Simulinkc = 4,000
4,000N

Knee bolts checked by hand

We checked the 10 mm steel knee bolts for bearing, shear and bending. With the safety factor applied, they still hold at 4,000 N.

10 mm

Designed part by part in CAD

Every part of V8 was modelled in SolidWorks before anything was printed or cut.

How it works

One file, sized to fit you.

You send us your measurements and we size the 3D design to your body. Then you choose: we print and build the leg for you, or we send you the files so you can print it yourself, close to home. That is how V8 can reach places where shipments can't.

  1. Step 1

    Measure

    Take your measurements with our step-by-step guide and send them in the order form.

  2. Step 2

    We adapt the file

    We check your measurements and size the V8 3D design to your body.

  3. Step 3

    We print it, or you do

    We print and assemble your leg, or we send you the sized files to print locally, with no customs and no waiting for a shipment.

  4. Step 4

    Fit & walk

    Snap the parts together, adjust the fit, and take your first steps.

Our mission

To give every person who has lost a leg a smart, strong and natural-looking prosthesis they can actually afford, made close to home.

Our vision

A world where losing a leg never means losing your independence, because a high-quality leg is affordable and can be made anywhere, from a single file.

Core values

What we stand for

Affordability

A smart leg from 150 JD, with a monthly option, so cost is never the reason to go without.

Quality & safety

Designed to clinical safety rules with a 1.5× margin. We say clearly that certification is still in progress.

Access for everyone

One file can be printed anywhere, so V8 reaches people even where shipments can't.

Repairable & sustainable

Replace only the part that wears out, at home. Nothing thrown away that still works.

Who we are

Three engineering students. One leg we built and tested.

We study engineering at Al Hussein Technical University (HTU) in Jordan. Together we designed, simulated, built and tested V8.

RA

Concept, execution & real-world testing

Came up with V8, drove it from idea to working prototype, and ran the real-world testing with an amputee.

Design & simulation engineer

Yazan Abdin

Design engineer & business lead

Worked on the engineering design and leads the business side of V8: the business model, pricing and growth.

Tested on a real amputee
